posts.post_title: Four common mistakes in heavy machine foundation design
posts.post_excerpt: Get one dynamic load parameter wrong and the whole line can vibrate past its allowable limit within six months of operation.
posts.post_content:
Foundation works for a 1,600-tonne stamping press at the Elektra plant, Lipetsk SEZ.

A heavy machine foundation is not simply a bigger block of concrete. It is a vibrating system with its own natural frequency, and the designer’s job is to keep that frequency well away from the equipment’s operating range.

1. Taking dynamic loads from the catalogue instead of measuring them

Manufacturer figures are nominal values under ideal conditions. On presses and crushers, real amplitudes can run 20–40% higher once the tooling has worn.

Strengthening a badly designed foundation typically costs four times what a vibration survey would have cost before the pour.

2. Ignoring frost penetration and seasonal soil movement

In central Russia the design frost depth reaches 1.6 m and the groundwater table moves a metre or more between spring and autumn. That changes the subgrade modulus and pulls the foundation’s natural frequency towards resonance.

  • Survey the ground in both seasons for any machine above 500 tonnes.
  • Design against a range of subgrade moduli, not a single average value.
  • Show a contingency piling option on the drawings.

3. Tying the machine foundation into the building foundation

It saves a few dozen cubic metres of concrete, then transmits vibration into the columns and cracks the cladding within a year or two. Always provide a wide enough separation joint.

Separation joint between machine and column foundations.
Reinforcement and anchor pocket of a press foundation before the pour.

4. Skipping vibration acceptance after commissioning

One measurement session with three accelerometers is enough to catch misalignment or under-torqued anchor bolts — before the line goes into real production.
